explanations.explanation: Both, friend. The writer says it's pleasing when you keep the words “…within you and they are constantly on your lips.” So they live inside you AND they come out of your mouth. Wisdom that never leaves the building is like a batch of cookies nobody's allowed to touch.

Not this time, friend. The writer says it's pleasing when you keep the words “…within you and they are constantly on your lips.” That's inside you and out loud, both together. So the statement is true just as written.

explanations.answer: So your trust may be in the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the goal, baker. The writer says, “So that your trust may be in the LORD, I instruct you today…” Every saying in this section points back to that one target. Not a trophy, not a crowd, just trust in the LORD.

explanations.answer: So your name will be remembered
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a nice goal, but the writer never says it. He says the instruction is “So that your trust may be in the LORD…” Nothing about statues or being famous. The goal is trust, and it's pointed at the LORD.

explanations.answer: So your barns will be full
explanations.explanation: Barns don't show up in this verse, friend. The writer says he instructs “So that your trust may be in the LORD…” A few sayings later he even warns, “Do not wear yourself out to get rich…” (Proverbs 23:4). So full barns aren't what he's aiming at.
That's the one. The writer says these words are given “…that you may soundly answer those who sent you?” That's how the verse puts it. The text doesn't say who sent you, so I'll leave that open, too.

That's a fair guess, but the verse doesn't name them. The writer says you'll “…soundly answer those who sent you?” No officials mentioned, no king. Kings do show up a few verses later, but in a different saying.

The gate is in the very next verse, so I see why that one tempted you. But this verse says you'll “…soundly answer those who sent you?” The elders aren't mentioned anywhere in this passage. The gate there is where the writer warns against crushing the afflicted, and that's a different saying.

The LORD, baker. The writer says, “…for the LORD will take up their case and will plunder those who rob them.” The poor man doesn't have to carry that case alone. Somebody bigger than any bully is on it.
Close to the gate, but not the answer. The verse says “…the LORD will take up their case…” No king in that line. Whoever is leaning on the afflicted should know who the writer says takes up the case.

The gate is mentioned a verse earlier, so I get why you went there. But the text says “…the LORD will take up their case…” The elders aren't in this saying at all. The case goes to the LORD, and He also plunders those who rob them.

explanations.answer: You may learn his ways and get caught in a snare
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. The writer says, “…or you may learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.” Notice the word "may." The danger he names is picking up the angry man's ways. I've picked up a few habits from the junk drawer myself, and I'm still shaking some of them.

explanations.answer: He may turn his anger on you someday
explanations.explanation: That could make sense, but it isn't the reason the writer gives. He says, “…or you may learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.” The danger he names is you picking up the angry man's ways. It's about what rubs off on you.

explanations.answer: You may lend him money and never get it back
explanations.explanation: Debts do come up soon, but in a different saying. For the hot-tempered man, the writer says, “…or you may learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.” The reason is you learning his ways. Pledges and security for debts show up a couple of verses later.

explanations.answer: Your own bed from under you
explanations.explanation: Your bed, friend. The writer asks, “If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?” That's a pretty rough picture. Imagine the debt collector showing up and the thing he wants is where you sleep.

The verse doesn't mention any animals. It asks, “If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?” The thing taken is the bed. Nobody's counting the flock in this saying.

explanations.answer: Your seat at the city gate
explanations.explanation: The gate does show up in this passage, but not in this verse. Here the writer asks, “…why should your bed be taken from under you?” It's your bed that goes. No gate seat, just the place you lie down at night.

Close, but the text doesn't give you that wiggle room. The writer says, “Do not move an ancient boundary stone which your fathers have placed.” No exception is given for needing more room. So the answer is False, and the stone stays put.

That's right, baker. The writer says, “Do not move an ancient boundary stone which your fathers have placed.” He doesn't add any exceptions for needing a little extra yard. The stone stays right where your fathers set it.

Kings, baker. The writer says the man skilled in his work “…will be stationed in the presence of kings; he will not stand before obscure men.” Good work gets noticed. I'd like to say my smudged cookies prove the same thing, but they mostly prove I have mustache problems.
Priests aren't in this verse. The writer says the skilled man “…will be stationed in the presence of kings…” It's kings who are named here. Skill in his work is what gets him there.

Prophets don't show up in this saying. The verse says the skilled man “…will be stationed in the presence of kings; he will not stand before obscure men.” Kings are the answer, and obscure men are the other side of the picture. Prophets are good company, but this verse didn't send them an invitation.

That's it. The writer says, “Do not crave his delicacies, for that food is deceptive.” He doesn't spell out how it deceives, and I won't make that up for him. The warning is plain: delicacies on a ruler's table, and the writer still says don't crave them.

explanations.answer: That food is for his servants
explanations.explanation: The verse never says that. It says, “Do not crave his delicacies, for that food is deceptive.” Servants aren't in this saying at all. Even the fanciest food on a ruler's table gets a warning label here, and I'd read it.

explanations.answer: That food is set aside for later
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the verse mentions saving anything for later. The writer says, “Do not crave his delicacies, for that food is deceptive.” The reason given is that the food is deceptive, not that it's being set aside. He doesn't say how it deceives, so I'll leave that open.

The text says the opposite, friend. The writer says, “Do not wear yourself out to get rich; be wise enough to restrain yourself.” So the answer is False. Getting rich isn't worth wearing yourself out.

You've got it. The writer says, “Do not wear yourself out to get rich; be wise enough to restrain yourself.” He doesn't say work is bad, but he says don't wear yourself out chasing riches. Restraint is the wise move here, and the writer says so.

That's the point. The writer says, “When you glance at wealth, it disappears, for it makes wings for itself and flies like an eagle to the sky.” You look, and it's already leaving. It's like trying to hold on to a warm cookie in a room full of hungry people.

It's an easy mix-up, since wings are in the picture. But the wings belong to the wealth, not to you. The writer says wealth “…makes wings for itself and flies like an eagle to the sky.” The riches are the ones leaving, and they don't take you with them.

explanations.answer: Riches come to whoever chases them
explanations.explanation: The picture goes the other way, friend. The writer says, “When you glance at wealth, it disappears…” The wealth makes wings and flies off, so it isn't something that stays with whoever goes after it. That's why the verse before says to “be wise enough to restrain yourself.”

That's what the writer says. The stingy man “…is keeping track, inwardly counting the cost.” He says, “Eat and drink…” but the writer adds, “…his heart is not with you.” The words say one thing and the inside says another.

explanations.answer: He's hoping you'll stay all night
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says is going on inside him. The writer says, “…he is keeping track, inwardly counting the cost.” His heart, the verse says, “…is not with you.” Staying all night isn't mentioned anywhere, but counting the cost is.

explanations.answer: He's getting ready to ask a favor
explanations.explanation: The writer never says anything about a favor. He says the man “…is keeping track, inwardly counting the cost.” The “Eat and drink…” is on the outside, but the verse says his heart is not with you. The cost is what he's thinking about.

True, friend. The writer says, “You will vomit up what little you have eaten and waste your pleasant words.” So the meal doesn't stay down, and the kind words you said are wasted too. It's a rough ending for a dinner invitation.

The text really does say it. The writer says, “You will vomit up what little you have eaten and waste your pleasant words.” The little you ate comes back up, and your pleasant words are wasted. So the answer is True.
Despise, baker. The writer says, “Do not speak to a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words.” Some folks hear good words and just roll their eyes. The writer says to save your breath.
That's the opposite of what the verse says. The writer says the fool “…will despise the wisdom of your words.” He doesn't treasure them. That's why the writer says not to speak to him.

Remembering would be a nice outcome, but that's not what the verse says. The writer says, “Do not speak to a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words.” Despising is what the fool does with them.

The fatherless, friend. The writer says, “Do not move an ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless…” The stone warning comes back with a new group added to it. So the stone and the fields both stay as they are.

Priests aren't named in this verse. The writer says, “Do not move an ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless…” The warning covers two things: moving the stone and encroaching on those fields. The fatherless are the ones whose fields are named, and the next verse adds, “…for their Redeemer is strong; He will take up their case against you.”

No king in this one, baker. The verse says, “Do not move an ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless…” The fields in question belong to the fatherless. Kings showed up earlier, but this saying isn't about them.

Strong, friend. The writer says, “…for their Redeemer is strong; He will take up their case against you.” The fatherless have a Redeemer who takes up their case. That's worth knowing before anybody moves a boundary stone.
The verse doesn't say that. It says, “…for their Redeemer is strong; He will take up their case against you.” Strong is the word the writer uses for Him. Nothing about Him being far off.
That's not what the writer says. He says, “…for their Redeemer is strong; He will take up their case against you.” The text calls Him strong. It doesn't say anything about slow.
The text says the opposite, friend. The writer says, “Do not withhold discipline from a child…” So the answer is False. This is one of the heavier sayings, so I'll just say it plainly.

That's right, baker. The writer says, “Do not withhold discipline from a child…” So he's saying not to hold it back. It's one of the heavier sayings in the passage, so I'll leave it at what the verse says.
